name: Carousel Studio
summary: Design six-slide carousels with a scroll-stopping cover, a locked visual system and sourced copy, from brief to export.
audience: Creators, marketers and small business owners who publish educational or news carousels.
needs: A text AI assistant and an image generator (ideally one that accepts reference images), or a design editor for art-plus-typesetting. Image tools, accounts and credits are separate.
includes: 12 staged prompts from research to export
Master brief, reference and slide worksheets
Editorial carousel example with caption, alt text and sources
sample: Create a reusable style block for [APPROVED ANGLE + BRAND + REFERENCES]. Specify canvas and safe zone, palette roles with hex values, headline/body/metadata hierarchy, image medium, material, light direction, texture, connectors, source/page-marker positions and avoid list. State what remains consistent and what varies. Offer one recommended direction, then repeat its style block verbatim for use in every slide prompt. Do not treat one creator's profile as one universal visual style.

name: Carousel Workflow Kit
summary: Specify a content queue, review steps and scheduled publishing without losing track of failed posts.
audience: Creators moving from manual posting to a reviewed publishing workflow.
needs: A text AI assistant. Implementing the plans requires your own automation platform and connected publishing accounts.
sample: Design a content queue for [CHANNEL] using [AUTOMATION TOOL]. Store draft_id, content_url, scheduled_at, timezone, approval_state, publish_state, external_post_id and last_error. Only approved rows may publish. Describe states and transitions, a duplicate prevention key, retry rules for timeouts and rate limits, and how an operator reconciles a post that succeeded remotely but timed out locally. Return a table and five acceptance tests. Keep credentials out of the queue. Do not publish anything.

name: 3D Website Lab
summary: Brief a purposeful 3D landing page with clear copy, six interface states and useful fallbacks.
audience: Designers, small studios and founders briefing a 3D-enhanced landing page.
needs: Your own page content, a developer or coding tool, browser, permitted assets and hosting if publishing.
sample: For [VISITOR], [TRUTHFUL OFFER], [PAGE CONTENT] and [NEXT ACTION], define a 3D landing-page job. Separate the attention role of the scene from the semantic explanation. Give a useful static fallback, six state requirements and a one-session prototype scope. Do not invent product facts, conversion results, ratings or a working deployment.

name: AI Video Direction Kit
summary: Direct six coherent shots with a visual treatment, continuity contract and practical take-selection gate.
audience: Creators and small production teams planning AI-assisted visual sequences.
needs: Rights-cleared references, an image/video tool with known controls, credits where required and an editor.
sample: Act as a director for [PROJECT] and [AUDIENCE]. Using [SUBJECT FACTS OR FICTIONAL INPUTS], [RIGHTS-CLEARED REFERENCES] and [DURATION BUDGET], define one visible promise, six shot jobs and the final attention target. Separate product facts from styling. State what cannot be claimed from concept art. Do not imitate a named filmmaker or invent a real product capability.

name: UGC Ad Script Kit
summary: Plan an honest short product ad with a clear hook, a visible demonstration and six visual boards.
audience: Solo sellers, creators and small teams planning product demonstrations.
needs: A product you can access, supplied product facts, rights-cleared presenter/media, an editor and optional AI tool access.
sample: Act as a product-demonstration director. For [PRODUCT], [AUDIENCE], [ONE VISIBLE TASK], [SUPPLIED FACTS WITH SOURCES] and [NEXT ACTION], write a one-page brief. Separate verified facts, fictional staging and missing evidence. Choose one observable demonstration and state what it cannot prove. Return a promise, production route, six scene jobs and explicit stop conditions. Do not invent experience, performance results, a discount or a destination.

name: Short Explainer Studio
summary: Explain one mechanism with a source map, a rehearsable script and six coherent visual scenes.
audience: Educators, product teams and creators explaining one small mechanism.
needs: A checkable topic, source material, an editor, a narration route and optional AI generation access.
sample: For [TOPIC], [AUDIENCE] and [SOURCE MATERIAL], define one question, a one-sentence answer and the exclusions. Separate sourced facts from [FICTIONAL EXAMPLE RULES]. Return an analogy map, six possible information changes and a final action. Mark unsupported statements; do not invent a study, product behavior or completed research.

name: Motion Briefs for Code
summary: Give a coding assistant a precise motion brief with scene timing, reusable variables and export checks.
audience: Developers creating title cards, launch clips or data animations with code.
needs: An AI coding assistant and your chosen animation framework. These are prompts, not finished video templates.
sample: Inspect the animation project and use its existing framework. Create a six-second title card for [TITLE] in [WIDTH x HEIGHT] at [FPS]. Define a single deterministic timeline: title enters at 0.4 seconds, supporting line at 1.2 seconds, both hold until 4.8 seconds, then exit by 5.6 seconds. Expose copy and colors as variables. Use licensed local fonts. Make arbitrary-time seeking produce the same frame as sequential playback. Return file changes and checks at 0, 1.2, 3 and 5.6 seconds. Do not claim a render exists until it has completed.

name: Lyric Visual Planner
summary: Plan exact lyric cues and a coherent original visual motif without inventing audio timing.
audience: Musicians, editors and creators planning text-led visuals with authorized material.
needs: Approved lyrics and audio permissions, an editor, actual timing review and optional image/video generation tools.
sample: For [PROJECT], [AUTHORIZED WORDS], [AUDIO STATUS] and [USAGE PERMISSIONS], create a lyric-visual brief. Preserve exact wording and identify the text authority. Define one emotional arc, motif and deliverable. If no recording is supplied, label cue order provisional and leave measured timing blank. Do not reproduce unprovided third-party lyrics or invent an audio performance.

name: Pixel Brand Prompt Kit
summary: Build an original pixel asset family with exact grids, transparent exports and a repeatable visual system.
audience: Designers, indie makers and small teams creating compact original pixel assets.
needs: A pixel-capable editor or the supplied source arrays, an application brief and your own final identity review.
sample: For [APPLICATION], [ORIGINAL SUBJECT] and [AUDIENCE CONTEXT], define a compact pixel identity study. Specify [NATIVE GRID], primary silhouette, supporting symbols and actual deliverables. Separate a fictional concept name from a cleared brand. Do not copy a game character, third-party mark or named artist's style, and do not promise commercial recognition.

name: YouTube Production Planner
summary: Plan a truthful title-to-payoff episode with six visual boards and an editor-ready production handoff.
audience: Solo video creators and small channel teams planning practical tutorials.
needs: A real episode topic, sources, recording/editing tools and your own channel access if publishing.
sample: For [AUDIENCE], [EPISODE TOPIC] and [AVAILABLE EVIDENCE], write one viewer question and the concrete artifact delivered by the video. Create a title expectation, thumbnail direction and opening payoff that agree. State exclusions and required recording. Do not invent audience demand, growth results or a finished video.

name: Video Shot Prompt Library
summary: Choose from thirty original B-roll briefs and adapt the right shot for a real edit.
audience: Editors, product creators and AI-video operators building a purposeful B-roll menu.
needs: A project brief, rights-cleared subjects, a video tool, any required credits and an editor.
sample: Using [EDIT OUTLINE], [AUDIENCE] and [LIBRARY PROMPT IDS], choose three candidate shots for [MISSING EDITORIAL JOB]. Explain what each adds, the neighboring shot, its likely continuity risk and a simpler fallback. Choose one first test. Do not claim an untested prompt is reliable, high-performing or compatible with every model.
